legislation.title: Telecommunications Act
legislation.content:
The Telecommunications Act enacted in 1993 as an Act of the Parliament of Canada that regulates telecommunications by ensuring reliable services, protecting privacy, and to protect and encourage the Canadian media. The Act is administered by the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) which reports to Industry Canada. It replaced the Railway Act of 1906, which governed telecommunication prior to 1993, making it the first full legislative scheme addressing telecommunications.
In this act, internet providers are considered utilities under this law in that they can't give "undue or unreasonable preference", nor can they influence the content being transmitted over their networks.

legislation.title: PIPEDA
legislation.content: The Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) became law on April 13, 2000, to promote consumer trust in electronic commerce. The Act was also intended to reassure the European Union that Canadian privacy law was adequate to protect the personal information of EU citizens.[1]

legislation.title: Bill-C13
legislation.content:
This Act, named “Protecting Canadians from Online Crime Act,” was introduced by Stephen Harper's Conservative government on November 20, 2013, and came into force on March 10, 2015[1][2].
Provisions in the Protecting Canadians from Online Crime Act include:
• Prohibiting the non-consensual distribution of intimate images.
• Empowering a court to order the removal of non-consensual intimate images from the Internet.
• Permitting the court to order forfeiture of the computer, cell phone, or other device used in the offence.
• Providing for reimbursement to victims for costs incurred in removing the intimate image from the Internet or elsewhere.
• Empowering the court to make an order to prevent someone from distributing intimate images.

legislation.title: National Security
legislation.content: This Act received Royal assent on June 21, 2019, and is a statute of the Parliament of Canada that restructured oversight of Canada's national security and intelligence agencies. It expanded the CSE’s mandate to include active and defensive cyber operations. Part V of this Act lays out changes to the disclosure regime between federal agencies, including limits on what information can be shared by agencies, as well as what privacy protections should be in place[1].

legislation.title: Broadband as a Basic Service
legislation.content: On December 21, 2026, the CRTC recognized broadband Internet access as a basic telecommunication service. It established an objective stating that Canadian residential and business subscribers should have access to speeds of at least 50 megabits per second (Mbps) download and 10 Mbps upload, and be able to subscribe to a service offering an unlimited data allowance[1].

legislation.title: The Internet Code
legislation.content: This Code was established by the CRTC and took effect on January 31, 2020. The Code protects consumer rights by requiring service providers to follow certain principles to ensure clarity in pricing, contracts, and offers, as well as facilitating the extension of services or switching service providers[1].

legislation.title: ACA
legislation.content: The Accessible Canada Act (ACA) came into force in 2019. The legislation benefits all Canadians, especially persons with disabilities, through the proactive identification, removal, and prevention of barriers to accessibility in seven priority areas, including information and communication technologies (ICT). This Act supports accessibility requirements for ICT products, including web pages, through the standard CAN/CSA‑EN 301 549.[1][2]

legislation.title: Online Streaming Act
legislation.content:
It received Royal Assent on April 27, 2023, and is the first major reform of the Broadcasting Act since 1991. The Act requires broadcasters, including online streaming services, to do a few things, such as[1]:
• Showcasing Canadian stories and music.
• Contributing to the production of Canadian stories and music in English, French, and Indigenous languages.
• Supporting a broadcasting system that reflects Canada's diversity.
• Helping to make programs accessible without barriers to persons with disabilities.
